 Special Executive Magistrate
 Last updated on October 31, 2026 by Swathi Satish 
 Special Executive Magistrates: Preventive Powers, Jurisdiction and Safeguards under the BNSS 
 In October 2026, a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) in Delhi ordered the release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka after seven days in judicial custody over proceedings related to alleged breach-of-peace bonds linked to a protest at Jantar Mantar.
 The development highlights the preventive powers of SEMs under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 , and the distinction between Executive Magistrates and Judicial Magistrates.

 Who Are Special Executive Magistrates? 
 Special Executive Magistrates are officers of the Executive branch empowered to exercise specified magisterial functions, primarily to prevent breaches of peace and maintain public order.
 Appointment and legal basis 
 Section 15 of BNSS: The State Government may appoint Executive Magistrates or police officers not below the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP), or equivalent, as Special Executive Magistrates.
 Specified jurisdiction: Such appointments may be made for particular geographical areas or specific functions and for a period determined by the State Government.
 Limited powers: An SEM can exercise only those powers of an Executive Magistrate that have been conferred upon them under the BNSS.
 Special arrangement in Delhi 
 Delhi has a commissionerate-based policing system.
 Under Section 70 of the Delhi Police Act, 1978 , the Central Government may authorise the Commissioner of Police and specified subordinate officers to exercise certain powers and duties of Executive Magistrates through official notifications.
 A 2010 notification authorised Assistant Commissioners of Police (ACPs) to exercise specified Executive Magistrate powers under Section 144 of the erstwhile Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, within their respective police subdivisions.
 However, this should not be interpreted as a blanket authorisation for every ACP to exercise all powers under the BNSS. The precise authority depends on the applicable appointment and notification.
 What Are the Major Powers of SEMs under the BNSS? 
 The BNSS provides several preventive powers to Executive Magistrates. An SEM may exercise only those powers specifically conferred upon them.
 Security for keeping peace – Section 126 
 An Executive Magistrate receiving information that a person is likely to commit a breach of peace or disturb public tranquillity may require that person to show cause why they should not execute a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace.
 The security period may extend up to one year .
 The provision is preventive and is not intended to punish a person merely for expressing dissent or participating in a peaceful protest.
 Preliminary order and inquiry – Sections 130 and 135 
 Section 130: The Magistrate makes a written preliminary order stating the substance of the information received, the bond amount, its duration and the sureties required.
 Section 135: The Magistrate conducts an inquiry into the truth of the information, following, as far as practicable, the procedure applicable to summons cases.
 During the inquiry, the Magistrate may require an interim bond or bail bond and detain the person until the bond is executed or the inquiry concludes, but only when immediate preventive measures are necessary and reasons are recorded in writing.
 The provision also contains safeguards against prolonged detention during the inquiry.
 Final order to furnish security – Section 136 
 If the inquiry establishes that security is necessary to maintain peace or good behaviour, the Magistrate may order the person to execute the required bond.
 The amount must be reasonable and proportionate to the circumstances of the case. It cannot exceed the amount or duration specified in the preliminary order under Section 130.
 Imprisonment in default of security or breach of bond – Section 141 
 Section 141 provides for imprisonment in two distinct circumstances:
 Failure to furnish security: A person ordered to provide security under the relevant provisions may be committed to prison if the security is not furnished within the prescribed period.
 Breach of an executed peace bond: If a person is proved to have breached a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace, the Magistrate may, after recording the grounds, order arrest and detention for the remaining bond period.
 This power is subject to the statutory requirements of proof and recording reasons; it is not an unrestricted power of preventive detention.
 Urgent prohibitory orders – Section 163 
 Section 163 empowers a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or another Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government to issue written orders in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger.
 Such orders may be issued to prevent:
 Obstruction, annoyance or injury to persons lawfully employed.
 Danger to human life, health or safety.
 Disturbance of public tranquillity.
 Riots and affrays.
 Orders may be passed ex parte in emergencies where prior notice cannot be served in time. They must state the material facts and satisfy the statutory requirements.
 Important: Section 163 does not automatically confer this power on every SEM. The officer must fall within the categories specified by the provision and possess the necessary authorisation.
 Release and discharge during preventive proceedings 
 An SEM may release a person detained during an inquiry when the statutory grounds for continued detention no longer exist. Under Section 137, if the inquiry does not establish the necessity of requiring security, the person must be discharged and released if in custody only for that inquiry.
 The BNSS also provides for the release of persons imprisoned for failure to furnish security under Section 142.
 These provisions must be distinguished from ordinary criminal bail proceedings, which are governed by separate provisions of the BNSS.
 What Are the Concerns Regarding the Powers of SEMs? 
 Threat to personal liberty 
 Preventive proceedings can result in detention without a conventional criminal trial. Their use therefore directly engages Article 21 , which protects life and personal liberty, and Article 22 , which provides safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention.
 The existence of statutory authority alone is insufficient; its exercise must follow a fair, just and reasonable procedure.
 Mechanical and stereotyped orders 
 The use of pre-printed or cyclostyled notices without assessing the individual circumstances can lead to arbitrary proceedings.
 A Magistrate must independently evaluate the material presented by the police rather than mechanically accept police allegations.
 Conflict of interest and institutional independence 
 When police officers perform both policing functions and magisterial duties, concerns arise about the independence and impartiality of preventive proceedings.
 The principle of Nemo judex in causa sua , no one should be a judge in their own cause, highlights the importance of institutional safeguards and independent scrutiny.
 Inadequate legal representation 
 Individuals brought before SEMs may not understand the nature of proceedings, the grounds for detention or their right to legal assistance.
 Lack of effective representation can undermine procedural fairness, particularly when preventive proceedings result in imprisonment.
 Financial burden of sureties 
 Unreasonably high bond amounts or insistence on financially unaffordable sureties can result in continued detention even after a person has been ordered to be released.
 The amount of security must be proportionate to the circumstances and must not become an indirect punishment for poverty.
 Risk of misuse against peaceful dissent 
 Preventive powers are intended to avert genuine threats to public peace.
 Their indiscriminate application against peaceful demonstrators, activists or critics can discourage legitimate participation in democratic processes.
 Judicial Safeguards: Aldanish Rein v. State of NCT of Delhi (2018) 
 In Aldanish Rein v. State of NCT of Delhi , the Delhi High Court examined the exercise of preventive powers by SEMs under the erstwhile CrPC.
 The Court found that the arrest and remand orders in the case were illegal and emphasised that preventive action must comply with constitutional protections and procedural fairness.
 Among its important directions and observations were:
 Reasoned orders: Magistrates must independently assess the material and record reasons before ordering detention.
 Right to legal assistance: Individuals must be informed of their rights, including the right to consult and be represented by a lawyer.
 Affordable sureties: Personal bonds and reasonable surety amounts should be considered to prevent detention arising solely from financial inability.
 Periodic review: The Court called for regular review of the necessity of continued detention.
 Oversight mechanism: It recommended consideration of an independent oversight mechanism, potentially involving retired judicial officers, to review the exercise of SEM powers.
 Accountability: The Court declared the detention and remand orders in the case illegal and directed compensation to the affected individual.
 The judgment is significant because it established that preventive powers cannot be exercised mechanically and must satisfy the requirements of Article 21 and Article 22.
 Its directions were issued in the context of the CrPC provisions then in force; their application under the BNSS must be read alongside the corresponding current provisions.
 Special Executive Magistrates vs Judicial Magistrates 
 Feature 
 Special Executive Magistrates 
 Judicial Magistrates 
 Legal basis 
 Section 15, BNSS 
 Section 9, BNSS 
 Appointment 
 State Government appoints Executive Magistrates or eligible police officers as SEMs. 
 State Government establishes courts after consultation with the High Court; presiding officers are appointed by the High Court. 
 Institutional position 
 Part of the Executive branch. 
 Part of the independent judicial system. 
 Primary function 
 Preventive action and maintenance of public order. 
 Administration of criminal justice. 
 Main jurisdiction 
 Specified preventive and executive functions conferred by law. 
 Criminal proceedings within their statutory jurisdiction. 
 Powers 
 May require peace bonds, conduct preventive inquiries and exercise other specifically conferred powers. 
 May conduct criminal trials, decide bail applications, issue warrants and impose sentences within their jurisdiction. 
 Independence 
 Subject to the executive hierarchy and statutory oversight. 
 Judicially independent, subject to the constitutional and statutory judicial hierarchy. 
 Role in criminal trials 
 Cannot conduct ordinary criminal trials or convict and sentence accused persons. 
 Exercises judicial powers in criminal cases, including trial and sentencing. 
 Colonial Legacy and Separation of Powers 
 The preventive jurisdiction of magistrates has historical roots in colonial-era legal frameworks, including the British Justices of the Peace Act, 1361 , which provided for preventive action against persons suspected of threatening public peace.
 In India, preventive provisions were incorporated into colonial criminal procedure and subsequently retained in the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. Several of these provisions have now been carried forward into the BNSS.
 The continuing use of police officers as SEMs raises questions about the separation of executive and judicial functions.
 Article 50 of the Constitution , a Directive Principle of State Policy, directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.
 While SEMs are constitutionally and statutorily distinct from Judicial Magistrates, the practical exercise of coercive powers by police officers requires safeguards against conflicts of interest and arbitrary decision-making.
 Way Forward 
 Strengthen independent oversight: Establish periodic review mechanisms involving judicial officers or independent authorities to examine detention orders and patterns of preventive action.
 Ensure reasoned and individualised orders: Every preventive proceeding should be supported by specific evidence, a clear apprehension of breach of peace and an assessment of whether less restrictive measures would suffice.
 Protect access to legal aid: Ensure that individuals are informed of their rights and have access to legal representation at the earliest stage of proceedings.
 Make surety requirements proportionate: Consider personal bonds and affordable sureties, particularly for economically weaker individuals, so that financial hardship does not result in unnecessary detention.
 Improve institutional accountability: Police officers exercising magisterial powers should receive specialised training in constitutional rights, procedural safeguards and principles of natural justice.
 Distinguish peaceful protest from genuine threats to public order: Preventive powers must not be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal investigation or as a mechanism to discourage lawful democratic participation.
 Strengthen judicial review: Courts should be able to examine the legality, necessity and proportionality of preventive detention and ensure that statutory safeguards are followed.
 Conclusion 
 Special Executive Magistrates perform an important preventive function in maintaining public order and averting disturbances. However, the exercise of these powers can directly affect personal liberty and fundamental rights.
 The distinction between Executive and Judicial Magistrates must remain clear, with preventive action governed by evidence, proportionality, procedural fairness and independent scrutiny.
 An effective rule-of-law framework requires the State to prevent genuine threats to public peace without compromising the constitutional rights of individuals.
